    Essay: Escape – MX

    📅 06 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 06.02.2026 in den Kategorien Opinion mit 3 Kommentaren.
    • A few thoughts and reflections on the analysis bubble.
    • According to recent reports, humans want to understand.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 06.02.2026 in den Kategorien Opinion mit 3 Kommentaren.

    A few thoughts and reflections on the analysis bubble.

    According to recent reports, humans want to understand. A fundamental need of our species eventually developed a concept for the desire to understand and to derive understanding: analysis. Carried through the centuries and applied primarily in literature, this drive increasingly found its way into the comparative physical activity of humans-sport. It fascinates hundreds of thousands of people every weekend; the urge to comprehend the logic – even where there is none – behind the results has become ever more omnipresent. Yet analysis existed long before people fully understood what analysis was – analyzing no longer becomes analysis simply because one is aware of doing it. Tracing the philosophical origins of analysis, pure analysis is merely a subform of communication: communicating by breaking down a whole into parts.

    If we understand analysis as part of a larger communication context, it is hardly surprising that analytical formats in Europe developed primarily through blogs and digital platforms – parallel to the ongoing technologization of the world. Analysis has always existed, but only with the internet did it gain fresh relevance: communication could, for the first time, reach a potentially unlimited audience permanently. This explains an apparent contradiction of its origins: analysis exists continuously, yet it is always dependent on its recipients. Without an audience, it has no effect. In the words of Niklas Luhmann, communication does not arise from mere sending, but from understanding on the part of the receiver. Analysis is therefore not an isolated act, but an interactive process.

    In the age of social media, however, this dependence increasingly leads to a dead end. Highly complex matters are expected to be made understandable, consumable, and entertaining within thirty seconds. Paradoxically, social media produces more recipients than ever – and simultaneously a structural scarcity of attention. Georg Franck refers to this as the “attention economy,” in which visibility, rather than truth or depth, becomes the central currency. For a long time, analysis was a dialogical process: presenting, structuring, weighing – a reciprocal interplay between sender and receiver, reliant on resonance and reflection. Jürgen Habermas’ concept of communicative action captures exactly this: understanding emerges where arguments are given time and space. In short-form formats, communication continues- often with enormous reach- but the channels through which it occurs have shifted.

    “A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.” – Herbert A. Simon.

    According to recent reports, analysis increasingly degenerates into a tool for tabloid-style exaggeration. Headlines such as “THE UPCOMING TACTIC,” “THE BEST PRESSING IN THE WORLD,” or “THIS IS MODERN FOOTBALL” suggest analysis but primarily follow market logic. Analyses are linguistically amplified as if they must be sold: the newest product, the best of its kind, faster, higher, further. Football as a consumer product is established – but now even the idyllic backyard of analysis? Marshall McLuhan’s famous dictum, “The medium is the message,” becomes particularly tangible here: the format determines not only the form, but increasingly also the content of analysis itself. The task is to reclaim analysis as a pursuit of understanding and curb its reduction to a consumable, attention-driven product – perhaps the challenge of the modern era is not to reinvent analysis, but to restore time, depth, and dialogical capacity to it.

    To continue the metaphor of the idyllic backyard: analysis is increasingly turning into a bustling city. Here a street vendor, there a shop – no, I don’t want to buy anything. Help, where have I ended up? Everything crowded, everyone stressed, everyone caught in the rush of striving, of wanting. I just want the idyll: a coffee, some calm, a deep conversation. But the idyll is dead. Perhaps, as an analyst, one sometimes feels a certain emptiness – a metropolitan melancholy – the emptiness of overstimulated impersonality.

    “The metropolitan is compelled by the economy of money exchange to a precision and objectivity that deprives personal life of its warmth.” – Georg Simmel, The Metropolises and the Intellectual Life, 1903.

    But let us zoom out again: I often experience this feeling on “X” or YouTube. There is an abundance of information, often highlighted for attention. Yet more information on complex topics does not automatically lead to more knowledge; it generates noise – a noise I described earlier in the metaphor. This constant noise simultaneously depletes the already scarce resource of attention and creates a perpetual stimulus environment, leading to a lack of contextualization and interpretation, while leaving many exhausted-another tactic video, another tweet, another reel on the best pressing? Phew – this “phew” is what science calls fragmented cognition. Algorithms naturally amplify extremes-even in sports: outrage, “ALL-CAPS HEADLINES,” or promotion drive engagement.

    This critique is not aimed at users or analysts; we are all trapped in a system with incentive structures. Nevertheless, I want to draw attention to the growing bubbleization and ideological polarization of the analysis scene, amplified by extremes and a lack of contextualization. Quick accessibility and democratization lead to information, to knowledge, but this abundance also produces a depletion of theory and balance. We experience a pseudo – plurality in sport, an implied logic in the game that does not exist, manifested by algorithms – through likes and views.

    A concrete example: relationism. A fascinating topic, scarcely explored-yet the mere word triggers algorithmic attention so heavily that it is used excessively, reducing it to a black-and-white concept and establishing a dogma, rather than allowing proper theoretical discussion. How do we get out of this situation? Everyone has taste, everyone has preferences – yes, everyone has their dogmas. We are human – accept it. As René Marić once remarked, dogmas can be dissolved by connecting them, by allowing different ideas to meet. Or as Jamie Hamilton puts it: perceive analysis as aesthetics. If we understand football as aesthetics, then football becomes art – but what is art? Art is the undefinable. And if we accept football as something without logic, we may at least free ourselves from established regimens of thinking and dogma. Don’t let yourselves be confined – feel the aesthetics.

    “We live in a world where there is more and more information, and less and less meaning.” – Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation, 1981.

    If we turn to history, literary philosophy shows us that even the concept of freedom divides opinion – does freedom enable analysis, or does it simply reinforce the status quo and thereby prevent true analysis? Perhaps, however, this is not the real question. Maybe it is not about freedom versus non-freedom, but about whether we understand logic as the opposite of freedom. Logicimplies binary outcomes – true or false, right or wrong – and this stands in tension with the ‘spirit of play’. Play has rules and objectives, yet within the act of playing there are no universal truths. The growing sense of uniformity and rehearsal – the impression that everyone plays in similar ways – often creates the feeling that the game follows the rules of a single, universal logic, as if logic determines play rather than play shaping logic.

    Recent findings suggest that my concern is less about what is objectively right or wrong in football, and more about how we, as analysts and coaches, sometimes present our ideas as universal truths. By doing so, we implicitly suggest that there exists a pure logic within the game – a logic that may not fundamentally exist. I would argue that sport exists primarily to evoke emotions in those who play and those who watch – an experience that can be understood through aesthetics, where art becomes a counterpoint to logic, as Tolstoy suggested. This challenges the belief that results or success should stand above everything else and dictate our styles of play.

    If there is no single ‘true’ way to play, then there can also be no single true analysis that fully dissects it into definitive parts. That is why we must give space to the diffuse edges – even at the risk of weakening clarity or precision in our explanations – and accept that not everything can be clearly identified or categorized, because pure logic does not exist here. Yet I firmly believe that by allowing more room for uncertainty and ambiguity within the game, we open ourselves to entirely latest worlds of understanding. And precisely for this reason, it is all the more notable to ask ourselves who we are-and what we want to be as analysts. We must no longer divide ourselves into “us” and “them,” but understand ourselves as a shared form of football observer. Hannah Arendt describes thinking as an activity that only unfolds in exchange, as something that emerges in the “in-between” of people. Analysis, therefore, is not a possession, but a process. We need to dare more again: recognize our own (natural!) weaknesses in reasoning, disclose our personal assumptions, and discuss more honestly with one another. Know more of what we do not know and never will.

    Recent findings suggest that for this reason, I am skeptical of sharply distinguishing between universally trained and didactically trained analysts – or of job advertisements favoring only one type. Pierre Bourdieu shows that fields tend to stabilize through differentiation rather than understanding; separation becomes a social marker rather than a question of quality. Class war! Is that really what we want? Pitting the professionalization of sport against an open culture? This runs all the way from coach education to analyst circles: those who were never professionals are excluded. Those who do not meet the standards in general education also do not meet the standards in football. It is a coupling of market logic with football – and we need a return to open football, even if this openness, in some places, requires a degree of self-criticism that is uncomfortable for some decision maker. Breaking out of established logics also means accepting that logic cannot be predetermined.

    “Technology is never neutral; it always changes the conditions under which knowledge is recognized.” – Neil Postman, Technopoly, 1992.

    In a recent development, attempts to standardize analysis this way lead to the imposition of linear thinking – a workflowization of analysis. The constant noise of information overload reinforces this effect. Increasingly, I observe a communicatively insulated bubble of club-based analysts, where external exchange is hardly desired. Yet the core of analysis is forgotten: “Thinking without communication is empty,” writes Jürgen Habermas-knowledge emerges in dialogue. Analysis thrives on joint dissection, on contradiction, and on critical (self-) questioning.

    This text is not a judgment of the scene. Rather, it is an expression of unease-a self-reflective judgment. I, too, have long allowed myself to be guided by factions, by the pursuit of jobs, by the pursuit of attention, and I became dependent on it. Only when I became aware of this and adopted a more didactic path – without a goal beyond curiosity about the game – did upcoming worlds of football open up to me. A curiosity expressed not in truths, but in provisional knowledge; in perspectives rather than dogmas; in theory as a tool rather than a label. Perhaps our strength should not lie in being faster, louder, or bigger. Perhaps it lies in withstanding the noise of the digital age. Where analysis no longer allows contradiction, it ends. But it also ends where analysis becomes mere consumption. But to end the text on a positive note – at the same time, there are more opportunities than ever before, more tactical cameras than ever, and more games to analyze than ever.

    It’s in our hands what we do with it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    West Ham United and Wales winger Ffion Morgan has had surgery on an anterior cruciate ligament injury and is now expected to sit out the rest of the 2026/27 campaign, a heavy blow for club and country with Wales less than a week away from a World Cup play-off final.

    According to recent reports, in a short injury revision published by West Ham, the club confirmed that the operation has already taken place and that the 26-year-old picked up the damage in the Women’s Super League home win over Charlton Athletic earlier this month. Morgan was helped off during that game, which Viviane Asseyi settled with two goals at the London Stadium.

    The Hammers said Morgan will now start her rehabilitation under the supervision of their medical staff, adding: “Everyone at West Ham United wishes Ffion a full and timely recovery.”.

    The timing makes the news even harder to take. As BBC Sport Wales reports, Morgan had just come back into the West Ham side after another lengthy absence, and this is not the first time she has faced an ACL rehabilitation. She also suffered an ACL injury as a teenager while on duty with the Wales Under-19s.

    Morgan moved to east London on a two-year contract in the summer of 2025 after her deal at Bristol City ran out. Before that she turned out for Crystal Palace, Coventry United and Cardiff City, and she is now a regular in Rhian Wilkinson’s Wales squads with 56 senior caps.

    Morgan was already missing from the 26-player group named for the two-legged World Cup play-off final against Norway. The Football Association of Wales squad announcement brought Ceri Holland, Hayley Ladd, Ella Powell, Rhiannon Roberts and goalkeeper Olivia Clark back from injury and recalled Gwen Zimmerman, but there was no place for the West Ham winger.

    Norway visit Cardiff City Stadium for the first leg on Tuesday 1 December (7:15pm), before the return leg at the Ullevaal Stadion in Oslo on Saturday 5 December. Both games are live on BBC Wales.

    Victory over two legs would not necessarily be the end of the journey. Only the seven best-ranked winners from this round go straight through to the 2027 finals in Brazil, while the eighth heads into the inter-confederation play-offs in February. Even if Wales do make it, Morgan’s recovery timeline leaves her a major doubt for next summer’s tournament.

    Wilkinson will now have to carry on without one of her most experienced wide players, while West Ham proposal for the rest of the season without a player who had only just fought her way back to fitness.

    Walter Sabatini non si aspettava di trovare Lazio e Roma ai primi due posti in campionato.     Sabatini, 71 anni, racconta anche delle proprie condizioni di salute dopo gli effetti delle migliaia di sigarette fumate: «Se senti un soffietto è perché ogni tanto mi attacco all’ossigeno, ma non ne avrei neanche bisogno».

    Industry observers note that alla domanda se avesse previsto le due squadre romane in testa, Sabatini risponde parlando prima della Roma e poi della Lazio. Attribuisce a Gattuso un lavoro sbalorditivo nella preparazione emotiva dei biancocelesti: «No. Era chiaro come la Roma fosse una squadra meravigliosa, destinata a vincere ogni partita per la determinazione, l’autorevolezza, la convinzione che la rendono quasi imbattibile.     Recent findings suggest that tra i giocatori cresciuti si sofferma soprattutto su Isaksen, dopo aver citato Belahyane e Noslin: «Penso a Belahyane, oggi invidiabile regista di copertura; a Noslin, attaccante che potrebbe giocare in qualsiasi club; a Isaksen soprattutto. All’allenatore affianca l’elogio del direttore sportivo Fabiani per le scelte di mercato: «Ha trasferito loro una parte del suo carattere, però smettiamola con la litania di Gattuso uguale Ringhio, solo grinta e basta.     Avendo lavorato come direttore sportivo per Lotito, Sabatini affronta anche il rapporto tra il presidente e i tifosi che lo contestano.     Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • James Trafford became the record signing for a British goalkeeper this summer and he is already proving invaluable for Leeds United.
    • Signed from Manchester City for an initial £40m in August, Trafford has made an outstanding start and frustrated Nottingham Forest twice in four days.
    • The England international secured his second successive clean sheet in this City Ground sequel to underline why Leeds moved to eclipse the previous record for Jordan Pickford.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    James Trafford became the record signing for a British goalkeeper this summer and he is already proving invaluable for Leeds United.

    Signed from Manchester City for an initial £40m in August, Trafford has made an outstanding start and frustrated Nottingham Forest twice in four days.

    The England international secured his second successive clean sheet in this City Ground sequel to underline why Leeds moved to eclipse the previous record for Jordan Pickford.

    “England’s No 1” was a frequent chant from the travelling Leeds fans and although it may take some time for him to dislodge Pickford as the country’s first-choice, he is loving life at his upcoming club.

    Trafford produced a number of fine saves and goals from Daniel James and James Justin secured a comfortable Carabao Cup second-round victory for Leeds, who also won here in the league on Saturday.

    Dan James has put Leeds ahead against Nottingham Forest 💥 pic.twitter.com/BdiYMXFJ5h.

    Leeds manager Daniel Farke stated: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

    “I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

    “He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”.

    Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

    Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

    Sources indicate that forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a latest right wing-back before the deadline.

    Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

    In a recent development, glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He noted: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

    “For nine months last season we were fighting relegation, so the players know it is going to take a lot of work. I know exactly what we have to change and that is what we will do.

    In a recent development, “We are responsible and made so many mistakes. Maybe we needed this result. At the moment we are far away from what we want but we will get there.”.

    This was a more open game than the attritional encounter from last weekend, as Trafford was forced into a fine early save to prevent Ola Aina’s cross from arcing into the top corner.

    Yet both teams were frequently making mistakes and providing masterclasses in how to misplace passes, frustrating their respective managers in the technical area.

    The most impressive moment of the first-half came from Leeds centre-back Joe Rodon, racing back into position to deny Chris Wood from close range. Rodon celebrated the tackle as if it were a 30-yard screamer.

    It was always likely to be a mistake which proved the pivotal moment, and Arnaud Kalimuendo’s poor header cost the home team in the 50th minute.

    Kalimuendo’s error presented Sean Longstaff with space to run into and his pass found James, who beat Matz Sels with a clinical finish.

    “Can we play you every week?” was the inevitable chant from the travelling Leeds supporters.

    Forest’s fans were becoming twitchy and Trafford produced another save to frustrate Wood from eight yards after a break down the right from Kalimuendo.

    Glasner responded by making a quadruple substitution on the hour, yet Leeds remained dangerous and added a second goal 15 minutes from time when Justin bundled home after a goalmouth scramble.

    Ethan Ampadu's long throw causes CHAOS in the Forest box as Leeds go 2-0 up! pic.twitter.com/CtGDDIaRNp.

    You can catch the draw for the next stage of the League Cup on Sky Sports Main Event tomorrow night after the conclusion of Preston North End vs Everton.

    Nottingham Forest have agreed a club-record deal worth £45m for Chelsea forward Liam Delap.

    Delap has been deemed surplus to requirements at Stamford Bridge, and while the clubs were in talks over an initial loan deal, they have now struck a permanent agreement for the striker.

    The 23-year-old​ only signed for Chelsea in a £30m deal from Ipswich Town 12 months ago​ ​and is scheduled for a medical on Wednesday​. He will become Forest’s most expensive signing with the deal eclipsing the £37.5m they paid for Omari Hutchinson last summer.

    Oliver Glasner has prioritised the addition of a new forward and Delap was a long-term target for the Austrian since his time as Crystal Palace head coach.

    Delap held talks with Forest last year over a potential move, and was also understood to have spoken with Glasner while he was at Palace.

    In a recent development, speaking to ITV after the win, Rodon stated: “I thought we were a bit sharper going forward, maybe a bit naive in the first half. I thought we had a lot of good chances maybe could have scored a couple of goals but we know it’s a difficult place to come and overall very happy to keep a clean sheet and win the game.”.

    Recent findings suggest that of his last-ditch tackle in the first half, he added: “We love it, as defenders it’s as good as a goal. I’m delighted, [keeping] clean sheets is my job and overall I got it right in the end.”.

    "There's a healthy arrogance about Leeds""Farke has gone from strength to strength"Izzy Christiansen and Jobi McAnuff praise the impact of Daniel Farke at Leeds 📈 pic.twitter.com/fgzLWRk3U2.

    "It's a bit soon to say Wembley!" 😅James Justin and Dan James react to Leeds progressing into round three of the Carabao Cup 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/m81C6eJT7C.

    Aug 30: Leeds United vs BrentfordSep 5: Brighton and Hove Albion vs Leeds UnitedSep 14: Leeds United vs Newcastle UnitedSep 19: Leeds United vs Crystal PalaceOct 10: Arsenal vs Leeds United.

    Aug 29: Liverpool vs Nottingham ForestSep 5: Nottingham Forest vs Tottenham HotspurSep 12: Aston Villa vs Nottingham ForestSep 19: Nottingham Forest vs CoventryOct 11: Crystal Palace vs Nottingham Forest.

    A tough night for the home teams...

    Cardiff City 1 Norwich 2Doncaster Rovers 1 Middlesbrough 3Barnsley 3 Crewe Alexandra 2Blackburn Rovers 1 Sheffield United 2Blackpool 1 Lincoln City 4Cambridge United 0 Millwall 1Fleetwood Town 4 Shrewsbury Town 0Ipswich Town 3 Leicester City 1Plymouth 2 Coventry City 4Sheffield Wednesday 0 Wolverhampton Wanderers 2Southampton 1 West Ham United 4Stevenage Town 0 Reading 3Stoke City 1 Hull City 1 (4-5 pens)Walsall 0 Leyton Orient 0 (5-6 pens)Watford 1 Peterborough United 5Birmingham City 1 Brentford 6Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds United 2.

    And that is it. Two home defeats by Leeds in less than 80 hours for Forest. Glasner will have much to ponder with a daunting trip to Anfield coming up on Saturday. All smiles for Farke’s side.

    A look at a third for Leeds. Aaronson drives forward before setting Wilson who in turn lays on a first-time pass to Calvert-Lewin. The forward attempts to take his shot first time but can’t get the requisite power on the ball to beat Sels.

    A pitch invader makes a brief appearance on the turf but is swiftly ushered away.

    There is a late chance for Forest. Hutchinson’s cross is helped on by Dominguez but that touch inadvertently takes the ball away from Ndoye at the back post.

    Forest fans are filing out of the exits and who can blame them?

    There will be six minutes of added time.

    In a recent development, that just about sums up Forest’s night. Dominguez stands over a free-kick from a dangerous area and, with the box loaded with their most imposing aerial threats, the midfielder sends the ball well over their heads and out for a goal-kick. So poor.

    According to recent reports, calvert-Lewin is now on for Nmecha. Not really the striker Forest defenders would want to see at this stage of the game.

    Another set-piece, this time a Stach corner, is barely dealt with by Forest.

    There’s a shout for a handball at the other end as Ndoye spears a cross into the body of Elvedi, but the referee rightly waves the appeals away.

    The “oles” ring out from the away end as Leeds string a series of passes together in the corner right in front of it. Forest are looking rather helpless here.

    Industry observers note that nottingham Forest 0 Leeds United 2 (Justin) Ampadu introduces a throw-in from the right but has to reload as the referee notices some pushing in the box. His next attempt is far too loopy but causes Forest all sorts of trouble, bouncing and bobbling, and coming all the way through a thicket of limbs to Nmecha at the far post. Williams attempts to keep the ball out from a prone position on the goalline under pressure from Justin, who gets the final touch as the ball is bundled over the line.

    Recent findings suggest that it's messy but Leeds won't care! 😁Forest fail to deal with the throw-in and Nmecha is there to bundle it in...#EFL | #CarabaoCup pic.twitter.com/oV46fs5RmP.

    Jair goes into the book after catching Ampadu in full flight. He never had a prayer of reaching that ball.

    The resulting free-kick lands to Amapadu himself in the box, but his effort is deflected behind for a corner which is not up to much.

    Goalscorer James is taken off for Bogle, who will offer more mettle down Leeds’ right side as Forest search for an equaliser in the closing stages.

    According to recent reports, stach has only been on the field for a matter of seconds but comes within a few inches of scoring. Wilson does well on the edge of the box before laying the ball to Stach whose curled effort grazes the outside of the side-netting.

    Longstaff’s final contribution to this game is a foul and yellow card as he spreads his legs wide to stop Ndoye breaking away through the middle.

    He is replaced by Wilson, as Tanaka and Okafaor also make way, for Stach and Aaronson.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s plenty more endeavour down Forest’s new-look left side. Hudson Odoi scampers down that flank before cutting inside, and while he’s unable to fashion a chance the intent is correct.

    The substitutions appear to have breathed life into this Forest side. Murillo picks out Dominguez charging forward and Trafford does well to tip the midfielder’s effort behind. The resulting corner comes to nothing.

    Glasner resolves he has seen enough and rings the changes. Diomande, Aina, Jesus and Kalimuendo are replaced by Murillo, Netz, Ndoye and Hudson Odoi.

    Okafor highlights off his dancing feet in the Forest box, pulling off a few stepovers before the ball comes to Ampadu on the edge of the area but his strike is dragged wide.

    Chances at both ends! Kalimuendo plays a wonderful ball into the box for Wood to sweep home but Trafford springs into action and makes a stunning save.

    Leeds go up the other end, Okafor profiting from a diversionary run from centre-back Elvedi but cannot find the target and double Forest’s lead.

    In a recent development, end-to-end football! ⚡️First Wood, then Okafor - just 19 seconds between the two chances 😮#EFL | #CarabaoCup pic.twitter.com/TGQmtwLNwE.

    Leeds are ahead and the inevitable chant from the away supporters is “can we play you every week?”.

    This is of course their second meeting in four days and Leeds are on course to record the double.

    Forest’s fans are starting to get a little twitchy.

    Sources indicate that dan James puts Leeds United in front! ⚽️Tidy finish from the Welshman... #EFL | #CarabaoCup | @LUFC pic.twitter.com/GzWg6zLGLm.

    Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds United 1 (James) We finally have a breakthrough. Kalimuendo gives the ball up cheaply in the middle of the park and Longstaff is there to pick up the pieces, darting infield before laying on a perfectly weighted for James to gallop on to, take a touch and sweep beyond Sels. The winger has been Leeds’ biggest threat and deserves that goal.

    James finds space down the right - again - and his cross is closed down and deflected behind for a corner.

    Longstaff’s floated delivery is tipped away by Sels, but it turns out that the ball went out before coming in so a Forest goal kick is awarded.

    A lovely rendition of Mull of Kintyre precedes a short blast of the referee’s whistle and we’re back under way...

    Schlager goes into the book instantly for grabbing a handful of Tanaka’s shirt as the Japan international attempted to escape his clutches.

    This hasn’t been much of an improvement from Saturday.

    Both teams are producing masterclasses in how to misplace passes. Oliver Glasner and Daniel Farke have spent much of the first half looking very frustrated.

    James Trafford must be feeling very comfortable and confident of a second successive clean sheet after joining from Manchester City.

    Let’s hope for an improvement in the second-half.

    Should the scores remain level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. There’s still a half to play of course, but Forest’s League Cup shoot-out record should be a source of confidence having won seven from eight.

    Leeds have only won four from 10.

    Sources indicate that what a tackle from Joe Rodon! 💥#EFL | #CarabaoCup | @LUFC pic.twitter.com/p5GkzSFEoZ.

    James wins the ball on the halfway line and feeds Okafor down the left. He attempts a deft through-ball into a thicket of bodies but it comes to nothing.

    Leeds circulate the ball, working the ball from side to side but there is nowhere near enough movement in front of the ball-player for any meaningful forward passes to be played.

    It has been revealed that and, quite aptly, the referee blows up at three seconds past 45 minutes. Certainly not a half for the books.

    Another half-chance for Forest! Milenkovic lands on a second ball off a deep free-kick but he cannot keep his strike down. A classic centre-half’s effort if you will.

    Ampadu comes over to the left to fire in a long throw-in. Sels comes steaming out of his goal and fumbles the ball but is awarded a free-kick after Muharemovic makes contact. Looked very minimal in all fairness.

    Oof, a good chance for Aina! Williams’ cross from the left comes all the way through to his opposite wing-back, but Aina’s half-volley sails over. A cracking contact, though.

    According to recent reports, elvedi and Muharemovic look to be astute buys from Leeds’ perspective. Both assured at the back and the latter especially is confident progressing the ball.

    Just as I type that Forest threaten with a ball over the top, but Justin nips in to take the ball away from Wood.

    Another decent opening for Leeds after a Forest turnover. Nmecha strides through the middle but Milenkovic is in position to ensure his run comes to nothing.

    What a tackle! Kalimuendo bursts through the middle after Leeds cede possession in a dangerous position. The winger plays in Wood who looks to be through on goal but Rodon comes out of nowhere to telescope a limb and stop the forward in his tracks. Fantastic defensive work from the Welshman.

    Nmecha attempts to break beyond the halfway line but is stymied by a swarm of Forest players. He demands a foul from the referee who is not interested in the least.

    It’s then Okafor’s turn to put in a dangerous cross from the left, but Nmecha cannot get to it.

    Tanaka becomes the first man to go into the book. The ball gets away from him and Jesus puts body between man and ball smartly to win the foul.

    According to recent reports, tanaka is now dropping into the back line to allow Leeds’ defenders the licence to get wider and higher. Forest will need to be wary of their opponents’ numerical advantage down the flanks.

    The game has reached something of a holding pattern as both sides resolve to slow things down, at least temporarily. Forest have settled into a slightly deeper block.

    Sensing an opportunity, Ampadu spins in a glorious through-ball between centre-back and full-back for James to gallop on to. He hits the by-line and cuts back to Longstaff, but the midfielder can’t beat Sels. A good chance that probably should have been converted.

    A good chance goes begging! 🫣Longstaff is free for Leeds but fires it straight at Sels...#EFL | #CarabaoCup pic.twitter.com/0UJdfSDQ6w.

    Tanaka then turns provider, winning possession in Forest’s half before playing in Longstaff, whose cross-cum-shot does not threaten Sels’ goal.

    Recent findings suggest that both sides have physical, quick out-balls, which has made for a frenetic encounter thus far. James rasps in another fierce cross from the right after another sweeping Leeds move, but Nmecha cannot get there and Tanaka fires well over on the follow-up.

    Aina’s throw-in, this time from the left, is flicked on to Jesus at the back post and while the forward is able to direct the ball goalwards there is Justin on the line to clear the ball to safety.

    Chance! Dominguez slides in Aina down the right channel and the full-back’s mishit cross has Trafford scrambling. He palms the ball behind for a corner, which is headed away for a Forest throw-in on the far side.

    Recent findings suggest that leeds are enjoying a spell of possession here, Tanaka and Longstaff peeling off into the wide areas to collect the ball and disrupt Forest’s mid-block out-of-possession structure. The hosts are more than happy for Leeds to circulate the ball in front of their first line of pressure as, for the second time tonight, Trafford boots it out into touch.

    Recent findings suggest that dominguez stands up a smart cross to the far post where Aina is waiting to head back across goal. Trafford backpedals into Kalimuendo and the referee awards Leeds a free-kick.

    Wonderful touch there early in the game from none other than Oliver Glasner.

    Forest’s head coach perfectly trapped a high ball as it landed towards him in the technical area.

    James shows off his speed for the first time tonight, accelerating down the right before fizzing a dangerous ball into the six-yard box but Forest clear their lines.

    Sels goes long to Wood (feels like the right play given his attributes), James lands on the second ball but can only boot the ball into row Z to jeers from the home fans.

    Aina releases a long throw-in from the right and it’s headed behind for a corner. Trafford punches the inswinging delivery away and Williams’ effort from the edge of the box sails well over.

    It has been revealed that forest are in their red home shirts, kicking from left to right. Leeds are in their yellow away number. Same set-up as the weekend.

    Recent findings suggest that players and mascots walk on to the City Ground turf. A place in the League Cup third round on the line.

    Recent findings suggest that the first pre-match question put to Glasner by ITV was in relation to the reported £45m club-record deal for Chelsea forward Liam Delap. He responded: “I can tell everybody that he doesn’t play today. Everything else we shall see in the next days.”.

    Oliver Glasner breaks his silence on Nottingham Forest's record signing, Liam Delap 🚨He speaks to @gabrielclarke05 ahead of Forest's Carabao Cup tie against Leeds 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/8DlWMIzVS9.

    It has been revealed that reflecting on Saturday’s defeat by Leeds in his programme notes, Glasner wrote: “I saw plenty of encouraging signs from the team on Saturday and I felt we were a lot closer to scoring than we were conceding, especially in the second half. Unfortunately, the small margins were not on our side.

    “I thought our defence looked comfortable, but there is still work to be done and the more the players get used to the system we’re operating, the more we’ll see that work come to fruition in competitive matches.

    “We have recovered well and will be ready to give our all this evening.”.

    Previewing tonight’s League Cup match, Leeds head coach Daniel Farke noted: “Our league win is good for our mood and confidence, but this is a ‘do or die’ cup game. Both teams will be motivated to progress, so I expect a tight game. It will be difficult to win on the road again against a tough opponent.”.

    Sources indicate that when asked what winning a first trophy of his managerial career would mean to him, Farke added: “Well, we weren’t too far away last season. Overall, I would say my form in cup competitions hasn’t been too bad during my career. I’m a significant believer in these competitions, I like the ‘do or die’ mentality. I would never say no to another good cup run.”.

    The hosts’ kits tonight will include Carabao Cup sleeve patches with the number four on them, in recognition of the club’s League Cup triumphs in 1978, 1979, 1989 and 1990.

    🏆x4⃣ pic.twitter.com/DRPXFa2kM3.

    This is Forest and Leeds Part 2, just four days after they clashed in the Premier League.

    Daniel Farke ruined the Oliver Glasner welcoming party on Saturday with a 1-0 smash-and-grab victory at the death.

    Both managers have gone relatively strong for this tie, with only a sprinkling of debuts.

    Ousmane Diomande, the £34m signing from Sporting, makes his first appearance while there is a first start for Xaver Schlager.

    Leeds have given a debut to Switzerland defender Nico Elvedi.

    Nottingham Forest Sels; Diomande, Jair, Milenkovic; Aina, Schlager, Dominguez, Williams; Jesus, Kalimuendo; Wood.

    Subs Victor, Murillo, Abbott, Netz, Hutchinson, Ndoye, McAtee, Sangare, Hudson Odoi.

    Leeds United Trafford; Rodon, Elvedi, Muharemovic; Ampadu, Tanaka, Longstaff, Justin; James, Okafor; Nmecha.

    Subs Perri, Lienou, Bijol, Bogle, Wilson, Cresswell, Stach, Aaronson, Calvert-Lewin.

    The big breaking news is that Forest are smashing their club record to sign Chelsea forward Liam Delap for £45m.

    Delap will undergo a medical at Forest on Wednesday with the deal potentially rising to £50m after add-ons.

    It eclipses the previous transfer record of £37.5m for winger Omari Hutchinson.

    Oliver Glasner has prioritised the addition of a upcoming centre-forward this summer and Delap ticks pretty much every box for him.

    Farke makes six changes to the complement that started against Forest in the league on Saturday.

    Wood makes Glasner’s XI while summer acquisitions Diomande and Schlager are handed their first competitive Forest starts.

    Our @Carabao_Cup XI this evening. 📋 pic.twitter.com/Wv918WJScj.

    Recent findings suggest that welcome to live coverage of the Carabao Cup second-round match between Nottingham Forest and Leeds United. This will be the sides’ second meeting at the City Ground in four days after Anton Stach’s late free-kick decided an attritional contest on the Premier League’s opening weekend. Forest’s new head coach Oliver Glasner is something of a cup specialist, though, with FA Cup, Europa League and Conference League titles to his name and he will relish the opportunity to right the wrongs of Saturday in front of the Forest faithful.

    It has been revealed that the Austrian is Forest’s fifth head coach in less than 12 months and he will look to arrest the churn by bringing to the City Ground the success he enjoyed with Crystal Palace. During pre-season, the Austrian moulded Forest into his preferred 3-4-3 shape, placing summer acquisition Ousmane Diomande alongside the existing central-defensive partnership of Murillo and Nikola Milenković. Here, Diomande gets his Forest debut and Glasner brings in talisman Chris Wood from the start.

    Daniel Farke will have been delighted to see his Leeds side continue their excellent form in pre-season – which included victories over Liverpool, Red Bull Leipzig and Augsburg – into the season proper. Although Leeds arrive at the City Ground shorn of attacking options Wilfried Gnonto, Noah Okafor and Mateo Joseph through injury, Farke still shuffles the pack in the forward positions with this weekend’s visit of Brentford to Elland Road in mind.
